turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: I -- I can --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: I think consistent with what you're saying is the way in which we in other cases have described Carlson. I mean, we didn't describe Carlson when we talked about it relative to the death being in a particular factor. We said things like -- and this is from Ziglar in 2017 -- that Carlson "allows a Bivens claim for prisoner mistreatment, specifically for failure to provide medical care." In Egbert, we said the same thing. In McCarthy, we said the same thing. We seem to be conceptualizing the Carlson level of inquiry at this higher state of generality, which is what you just said in response to Justice Alito.

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: I agree with that, Your Honor. And it's particularly significant, again, because Congress has legislated in response, right? At the time Congress is passing the PLRA, it knows that McCarthy was a Carlson case where there was no death, where there was no acute emergency, and this Court was declining to impose an administrative exhaustion requirement. So Congress, in passing the PLRA, understood the class of Carlson claims that were being brought yet, instead of overruling it, erected a procedural structure around it. Same at the time of the Westfall Act. Again, for the vast better part of four decades, there's never been any question among the lower courts that a claim like Mr. Watanabe's arose in the prototypical Carlson context. That dispute came about only over the past few years after some courts, we believe, have started to misinterpret this Court's decision in Egbert as essentially foreclosing all of these claims. So this has not proven, actually, to be an unworkable or challenging exercise up until recently.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: I wanted to follow up on Justice Kagan and Justice Alito's question about why is death different. You explained why reckless -- negligent -- medical negligence is the very essence of an Eighth Amendment substantive issue. Was someone intentionally and deliberately inflicting pain and suffering or -- or non-treatment on a prisoner? And so that's going to get addressed in -- in that prong of the question, correct?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: But, on the "death is different," why don't -- isn't that the same thing?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: I think it is also the case that there's a conceptual mismatch between using "death is different" as a distinguishing factor and the substantive Eighth Amendment claim that is being brought here because the remedy or -- sorry, excuse me -- the injury that's being remedied there is the pain and suffering attendant to the deliberate indifference, not the ultimate consequence, right? It is the actual suffering that has occurred. And it also runs into the deterrence problem.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So what does it matter -- I think Justice Kagan asked earlier -- if you ignore systems -- systems for a period of time and somebody suffers a heart attack and is permanently disabled, what does it matter to them if they died or are permanently disabled? The indifference was the same, correct?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: And I think, actually, for Eighth Amendment purposes, we would describe that violation as more egregious, not less, because it extends the pain and suffering even further, and --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well, wouldn't it -- I'm sorry, finish your --

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: No, please.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: No, I didn't mean to interrupt.

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: Just that that is another way, I think, in which there's a mismatch between the substantive standard and the distinction that they've offered here.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: What do you think it would --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Oh, I'm sorry, go ahead.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: I was just going to say I -- I wanted to make sure I got that right. You're saying it was more serious if the person didn't die?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: For -- not more serious, but, for purposes of the Eighth Amendment, what the -- what the Eighth Amendment is concerned with is the pain and suffering that leads up to the death, not the death itself. And so for them to draw the line in this way I actually think is kind of backwards as a matter of Eighth Amendment law.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: So -- but I guess my question's the same: You think it's a more serious violation if the person doesn't die?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: It's a more serious constitutional violation, but -- but -- but --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Still, death is a little --

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, I mean, as a -- as a matter of sort of common sense and tort law, yes, I would say death is very significant. But the problem is the mismatch between the Eighth Amendment and the distinction that they're drawing.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well, do you think it would be irrational for Congress to think, on the one hand, we want to provide a remedy for really egregious instances of medical malpractice perpetrated on prisoners, but, on the other hand, we understand that prisoners are very litigious and may have all sorts of complaints against the doctors and the nurses who provide them with care, so we're going to draw a distinction between situations where the prisoner actually dies and other situations? As Justice Kagan said, it's a hard line, but do you think it's an irrational line when they're potentially balancing competing objectives?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: I don't think it would be an irrational line for a hypothetical Congress to do that. But I think we should start by asking ourselves: What has Congress actually done here, right? When it passed the Westfall Act, there was no notion that Carlson was limited to claims in which the prisoner died. And yet Congress still took the additional step, after enacting a -- an extensive and sweeping preemption provision, to then except from that Carlson claims and Bivens claims. And then, in the PLRA, again, Congress set up an administrative exhaustion scheme that only makes sense for Carlson claims if claims can be pursued by prisoners who did not die from their injury. So, yes, I understand that -- that that is a possible route that Congress could go, but I think we should be focusing on what is it that Congress has actually done and told us in this area about what types of claims it thinks are sustainable.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Counsel, you -- you indicated that up until Egbert, you thought the lower courts were pretty clear about how to apply this two-step regime, but since then, there's been a fair amount of confusion, is that right?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: I think, with -- with respect to Mr. Watanabe's claim, I mean that it has not seriously been disputed that a claim like this arises in the prototypical Carlson --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: But now there is a fair amount of confusion because we said in Egbert to ask whether there's any reason to think Congress may be better equipped. You think that standard has proven difficult for lower courts to deal with?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: I think it has. And I think also the Court's statement that the two steps sometimes collapse into each other, which I believe is correct but for a different reason than my -- than my friend does.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: But you think that's generated confusion in the lower courts?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: I -- I do, Your Honor, yes.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay. And then I'm just curious: Your client, I understand, was proceeding pro se --

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- and did not bring an FTCA claim if I --

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: That is correct.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: And do you think part of that might be because -- because of confusion about which is the best route and how to proceed in these cases, that -- that the pro se litigants sometimes don't know about FTCA claims?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: I think a large problem is the -- the pro se litigants not knowing about the FTCA claims and also not knowing how to navigate the administrative procedures that you have to go through in order to assert an FTCA claim. There are obviously administrative exhaustion requirements for a Carlson claim, but those are within the walls of the prison. Everybody understands how those work at a general level. And I think there are practical challenges with pursuing an FTCA claim on a pro se basis.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Counsel, you agree that Congress could eliminate Bivens actions tomorrow if it wanted?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: That is our understanding of the precedent. And, yes, we agree with that.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Okay. One other question. Your friends on the other side point to the PATRIOT Act as a subsequent legislative development. And I confess, on the question of whether that's an alternative remedy and a cause of action, I don't find the existence of that statute really neither here -- I think it's neither here nor there. But you were emphasizing deterrence before and the importance of Bivens actions in deterring unconstitutional conduct by prison officials. The PATRIOT Act, as I understand it, does tighten up prison regulations and provide for discipline of officials that do violate regulations in federal law. Would that bear on whether it's appropriate to have a Carlson remedy here given that there are other mechanisms Congress has put in place for purposes of deterrence?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: Well, so two things. First off, I think I understand the PATRIOT Act to apply simply to all Department of Justice divisions, which include the Bureau of Prisons but is not specifically narrowed to that. But I -- I do think that this Court has recognized over time that there is something uniquely powerful about the threat of individual liability that serves an important and additional deterrence purposes. We're not suggesting that Carlson is the only thing out there that prevents officers from acting unconstitutionally. Of course, there's many other motivations for doing that. But this Court has consistently recognized that this type of claim has a special role in that place. And I -- I think it's especially important for a plaintiff of this type. Prisoners have been long understood as uniquely vulnerable within our common-law tradition, and there's unique responsibilities and obligations on the jailer that flow from that. And so, if we're going to hold deterrence up in any place, I think it has to be in this context, where we know these individuals are uniquely susceptible to constitutional violations.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: I also think the other mechanisms analysis sort of proceeds on the assumption that Congress only wanted there to be one way to go about this. And I'm just wondering how viable or justified is that assumption?

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: I don't think it's -- I think it's actually contradicted by the Westfall Act because Congress is clearly contemplating there that there's going to be two remedies. There's going to be the FTCA and there's going to be the constitutional claim. So I wouldn't just say it's unsupported. I think it's actually foreclosed by what Congress has done. And -- and I would add also to that the PLRA, which describes administrative remedies as a prerequisite to and not a substitute for other claims, such as a Carlson claim or a 1983 claim.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Thomas? Justice Alito, anything? Justice Sotomayor? Justice Kagan? Justice Kavanaugh? Justice Barrett? Thank you, counsel.

turns.name: JOSHUA M. WESNESKI
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Rebuttal, Mr. Walker.

turns.name: LUCAS M. WALKER
turns.text: Thank you. So my friend challenged the idea that this should be looked at from a legislative perspective, that a difference is meaningful if Congress could think that it's meaningful from a policy perspective. But I think that's exactly the principles this Court articulated in Egbert and all of those other cases preceding it. This is a legislative endeavor that has to be performed with the utmost deference to Congress. It requires considering policy considerations that Congress is far better suited to weigh and the judiciary has questionable authority at best to weigh. Those are paraphrases or quotes from Egbert itself. And if a court is a saying we're not going to get to the question of whether Congress might be better suited because there's a difference here, Congress might think that it's meaningful, but we don't think it's meaningful, I think that just sets up the exact separation-of-powers problem that the framework that this Court has set up is trying to avoid. Yes, it may be a bit of a patchwork, but that's because the Court has been trying to get back and back and back to the proper approach, which is that Congress is really supposed to be making all of these damages remedies decisions. I believe my -- my -- my friend admitted that if the test is whether Congress could find a meaningful difference, that those exist here. "Damages or nothing" is something this Court has found meaningful. Alternative remedial structures and other signs that Congress has been active in this area without providing a remedy, those exist. This Court has already found them meaningful. The suggestion that it's just -- it's the same right and it's the same mechanism, therefore, it's the same context, is something the Court rejected emphatically in Ziglar, specifically in the context of Carlson claims. I think it's page 147 of that decision. Here, we've got all sorts of differences. The question of whether death is a meaningful difference, deterrence is supposed to be the sole concern of Bivens. But Egbert tells us that deterrence is something that Congress is supposed to calibrate. And we've seen in statute after statute that when it calibrates appropriate deterrence, the fact that death resulted or didn't result is very often something that results in enhanced deterrence or not. That is a meaningful difference, and I think that alone -- in addition to the other ones that we have here. How the Court has previously described Carlson, Carlson's first sentence says that the inmate died. In Minneci, the Court described Carlson as one where he had died as a result of the violation, and as a result, there was no state damages remedy. So the Court has described it in those more granular terms as well. The Westfall Act, it doesn't affect the new context inquiry at all. That's what Hernandez said. And so all those meaningful differences are proper to find that this is new context. But, as the question as to whether it would prevent overruling Carlson and Bivens, I believe my -- my friend abandoned any argument that it constitutes a ratification. He's relying just now on a reliance argument. But that rests on the -- on the -- the premise that Congress thought it was taking away something, a common-law tort liability against individual officers. The findings enacted in the text of the statute say Congress thought there was no liability. There was already a remedy in place that this Court's Westfall decision had eliminated, And all Congress was doing was restoring that wall, ensuring a damages remedy against the United States.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted.
